name: Watercolour
basis: why: thin pigment over white paper can only darken, bleeds, dries in rims; how: bleed blur, wet wobble, granulation, edge pooling

lumenary.blurb: Thin washes of pigment on rough paper: soft bleeds, darker rims where the colour dried, and a little granulation.

facts.era: Centuries old, English school of the 18th and 19th centuries

why: Watercolour is thin pigment carried by water, so the white of the paper shows through it and a stroke can only ever darken what lies beneath. That one fact explains the whole look: bright areas are simply left unpainted, colours bleed into one another, and pigment pools in dark rims where a wash dried. This treatment works in pigment laid over a paper colour for exactly that reason.
how: Blur the picture by an amount set by the bleed slider to stand in for water spreading.
Read it from slightly displaced places, nudged by slow noise, for the wobble of a wet brush.
Pull each channel part way toward the nearest of seven levels, because washes settle in flat tonal steps.
Compute pigment as darkness times small effects: nothing in the lightest areas, uneven blooms from broad noise, granulation from fine noise, and pooling at edges.
Darken the paper with that pigment, then add an optional unpainted border and a faint fibre pattern.
history: Painting with water-based colour is ancient, but the English school of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with artists such as Thomas Girtin and J. M. W. Turner, made it a major art of landscape. Albrecht Dürer had already painted detailed watercolour studies of plants and animals around 1500. Portable paint boxes later put watercolour in the hands of travellers and amateurs.
uses: Soft wall art and book covers
terms: A thin, even layer of watery paint.
Pigment that settles into the hollows of the paper and gives a speckled texture.
Painting onto paper that is still damp, so colours spread and blend.
paragraphs: A watercolour wash is thin pigment carried by water. You see the paper through it, so a stroke can only ever darken the white underneath, and the program works in pigment (how dark each colour channel is) laid over a paper colour. The picture is first blurred, with a radius of 2 to 11 px set by the bleed slider, to stand in for water spreading. Each pixel then reads that blurred picture from a place nudged by slow noise (about ±3.5 px), the wobble of a wet brush, and each channel is pulled 55% of the way toward the nearest of seven levels, because washes settle in flat tonal steps.

The pigment at a pixel is the darkness times a handful of small effects. Very light areas get nothing at all, since a painter leaves the paper bare for the highlights. Broad noise (±21%) makes the wash bloom unevenly, and fine noise makes the pigment granulate, settling in the hollows of the paper. Where the picture has an edge the pigment pools, as it does at the rim of a drying wash, and the dark rims slider controls how much. The result darkens the paper colour; an optional unpainted border with a ragged inner edge, and a faint fibre pattern, finish the sheet.

equations.note: Each channel v (0 to 1) of the blurred picture is flattened toward seven levels.

s is the colour strength (0.45 to 1.2), ℓ = 1 − smoothstep(0.8, 0.97, L) the lift that keeps highlights bare, b bloom, g granulation, ρ the rim slider and e = smoothstep(0.015, 0.09, edge strength) the pooling at edges.
The pigment only darkens the paper beneath it, channel by channel.

presets.text: High bleed and light colour make a loose, dreamy wash.
Strong rims with rough paper look like a quick plein air sketch.
Turn off the border to let the picture fill the page.
